audio_script: A ball drops from a shelf. Its speed grows, but where did that motion come from? Choose the ball and Earth as one system. At the top, the system has gravitational potential energy, mass times gravity times height. As the ball falls, its height decreases and so does that energy. Gravity speeds the ball up, increasing its kinetic energy. If air resistance is negligible, the decrease in potential equals the increase in kinetic. For a two kilogram object dropping five meters near Earth's surface, m g h is about ninety-eight joules. The bars show an exchange, not energy appearing from nowhere. On the right, plot potential as a function of height and you get a straight line. Kinetic energy is the mirror image. Their sum stays flat. That flat line is conservation. But the accounting is exact only if you choose the system carefully. Include the air and some energy becomes heat. Include the Earth and potential is well-defined. Exclude either and the ledger breaks. This is why physics begins with the system. Define what is inside, name your assumptions, then follow every transfer across the boundary. The claim of conservation is not that the number is visible. It is that after all the complicated machinery runs, the total is unchanged. Energy conservation is less a magic equation than a disciplined way of tracking change.

The officer is not claiming she covered sixty miles. He is claiming that if she kept going at that rate, she would. That is the entire idea of instantaneous speed, and it took centuries to make it precise. Measure where the car is at one time, then at a slightly later time. Divide distance by elapsed time. That is average speed, and it depends on which two times you pick. Now shrink the interval. The average settles toward a limit. That limit is the instantaneous speed. Look at the graph on the left. The yellow secant joins two points on the curve. As the interval shrinks, the secant rotates. It approaches a single line tangent to the curve at one point. audio_script: A puck sliding on frictionless ice keeps moving after the push ends. That can feel strange if we expect motion to need a force. Newton's first law says an object keeps constant velocity when the net external force is zero. A net force changes velocity. The change per unit time is acceleration. Newton's second law writes this as net force equals mass times acceleration. But read it carefully. The law is not a definition. If it were a definition, physics would be empty. The law is a program for studying nature. It says that when you compute mass times acceleration and call the result force, you will find that forces are simple. Newton himself gave one such force, gravity. For everything else, we study forces case by case. Now, a projectile. On the right, a ball is launched at fifty-five degrees. Its path is a parabola. Why? Because two independent things happen at once. Horizontally, no force, so constant velocity. Vertically, constant gravity, so constant acceleration. Combine them and the trajectory curves. On the left, the initial velocity is decomposed into horizontal and vertical components using vector addition. The vertical component shrinks under gravity. The horizontal component stays fixed. Every point on the parabola has the same horizontal speed as the launch. This is why the path is symmetrical. It is not that a hidden force pulls the ball forward. It is that nothing slows its horizontal motion. Newton's second law is a claim that the forces you find will be understandable. That is its real content.

tagline: It depends on where the mass is

audio_script: A solid disk and a thin rod. Same mass. Same torque applied. The disk spins up quickly. The rod turns slowly. Why? Because mass alone does not determine how a body resists turning. What matters is how far the mass sits from the axis. The moment of inertia is the sum of each bit of mass times its distance from the axis, squared. For a uniform disk about its center, inertia equals one half m R squared. For a rod pivoted at one end, inertia equals one third m L squared. Notice the radius, or the length, is squared. A body with mass spread out has a larger moment of inertia, so the same torque produces less angular acceleration. In the animation on the left, the disk. On the right, the rod. The red marker on the rim traces its own velocity arrow, which is the tangential speed. That arrow is omega times the radius. On the rod pivoted at one end, the far tip moves much faster than the pivot. This is why a door handle is placed far from the hinge. This is why a long pendulum swings slower than a short one. And this is why an ice skater who pulls in their arms spins faster. The mass has not changed. Only the arrangement has.

tagline: Continuous fall around a curved Earth

audio_script: A satellite is not beyond gravity. It is falling toward the Earth all the time. So why does it not hit the ground? Because it also has sideways velocity. As gravity bends its path inward, the satellite moves forward enough that the curved Earth falls away beneath it. An orbit is a continuous fall that keeps missing. For a nearly circular orbit, gravity supplies the inward centripetal acceleration, v squared over r. This is not a balance between gravity and some outward force. In an inertial frame, gravity changes the direction of velocity, and that is all. The trail shows the path. If the satellite moves faster, it climbs to a larger orbit, where the required centripetal acceleration is smaller. The circular speed at radius r is the square root of G M over r. Notice: the mass of the satellite drops out. A pebble and a space station at the same radius would follow the same path if given the same velocity. That is a deep hint about gravity. It couples to mass in exactly the way inertia measures mass. This equivalence, checked to one part in a trillion, is the seed of general relativity. Real orbits also experience drag, tides, and perturbations from other bodies. The simple ellipse is an idealization. But the geometric picture, sideways motion plus continuous inward acceleration, is the intuition that survives.

You would expect a bigger displacement to take longer. But it does not. Why? Because the restoring force grows with the displacement. Twice as far means twice the force. Twice the force means twice the acceleration. Twice the acceleration covers twice the distance in the same time. The time pattern is fixed by the system, not the amplitude. Write the law as m times acceleration equals minus k times displacement. Divide by mass and you get a simple differential equation. Its solution is a cosine. The frequency is the square root of k over m. A stiffer spring oscillates faster. A heavier mass oscillates slower. The animation shows a mass on a spring. Its motion traces a cosine curve on the right. The same cosine shows up in electrical circuits with inductors and capacitors, in molecular vibrations, in the swinging of a pendulum for small angles, and in the light emitted by an atom. Any system whose restoring force is proportional to displacement obeys this equation. This is why the harmonic oscillator is everywhere in physics. audio_script: When a force pushes an object, the object gains kinetic energy. How much? If the force is constant, work equals force times distance. But what if the force varies? Then we cannot just multiply. Imagine stretching a spring. As you pull, the force grows. Near the start, little force. Near the end, a lot. So how much work is done? Break the displacement into small steps. Over each small step, the force is roughly constant. Multiply the local force by the step size. Add up all these products. That sum is the work. As the step gets smaller, the sum becomes an integral. On screen, the rectangles approximate the area under the curve. Ten rectangles. Then a hundred. Then infinitely many. The exact work is the area under the force-versus-position curve. For a spring, this integral equals one half k L squared, where L is the total stretch. This is the elastic potential energy. It matches the kinetic energy gained by the spring when it is released. So work and energy are two views of the same physics. The work-kinetic energy theorem says the total work done on a body equals its change in kinetic energy. Integrals are how we compute work when the force varies. Derivatives are how we compute force when energy is known. The two operations are inverses. That is the fundamental theorem of calculus, and it is the language of mechanics.

audio_script: A vector is not just three numbers. It is an object that transforms in a specific way when we change axes. That definition is what makes the physics work. But most of the time we use vectors without thinking about transformations. We add them tip-to-tail. We scale them by constants. We decompose them into components. So far, these are all simple. Now consider a new operation. Given two vectors, we can combine them into a single number. This is the dot product. Geometrically, it is the product of their lengths times the cosine of the angle between them. It measures how much one vector points along the other. Think of it as a projection. If they are perpendicular, the cosine is zero, so the dot product is zero. If they are parallel, the dot product is the product of the lengths. Algebraically, we compute it by multiplying corresponding components and adding. That formula looks unrelated to the geometric one, but it is exactly equivalent. On the left, two vectors being added. On the right, the same vectors, with the dot product displayed. Where does this matter in physics? Work is force dot displacement. Flux is field dot area. Power is force dot velocity. The dot product is the standard way to turn two vectors into a scalar. It is one of the most used operations in all of physics, from mechanics to electromagnetism to quantum theory.

audio_script: A car travels sixty kilometers in the first hour and ninety kilometers in the next two hours. What is its average speed over the whole journey? The average speed is the total distance divided by the total time. Total distance is sixty plus ninety, one hundred fifty kilometers. Total time is one plus two, three hours. Dividing, we get fifty kilometers per hour. Option A. Notice that we do not simply average the two speeds. If we did, we would get seventy-five kilometers per hour, which is wrong. The car went at different speeds for different amounts of time. So we must weight by time. The correct definition of average speed is total distance divided by total time. Whenever you see average speed, remember: total distance over total time. Everything else follows from it.
